title: Hundreds more
hookLine: the Masnavi has hundreds of stories, and we read about twenty
tomorrow: camp 4 close: the reed and the emperor

lines: ONE SHELF, AND IT WAS THE LOBBY.
cards: A visitor finishes one shelf of a huge old library, heads for the exit, and the librarian at the door says: that was the lobby. That's where this camp stands with Rumi.
About twenty of his stories so far: the reed, the parrots, the lion, the harper, the shepherd, the chickpea, the painters.
But the Masnavi runs to six books of verse, and it holds hundreds of stories, many nested inside each other. The door has barely opened.

teach.b: Here's a taste of what's waiting, all from book one alone. A proud grammarian gets into a boat and asks the boatman, have you ever studied grammar? No, says the boatman.
Then half your life is wasted, says the grammarian. The boatman goes quiet. Then a storm rises, and the boatman asks: have you ever learned to swim?
No, says the grammarian. Then all your life is wasted, because the boat is sinking. Rumi's point, drawn out over many lines: in the deep water, cleverness about words won't hold you up.
What saves you is emptying yourself, becoming like the dead, who float. A man from the city of Qazvin goes to a tattoo artist and asks for a fierce lion on his shoulder.
At the first prick of the needle he cries out: which part are you doing? The tail, says the artist. Leave off the tail.
Then the ear. Leave off the ear. Then the belly.
Until the artist throws down his needle: who ever saw a lion with no tail, no head and no belly? You want to be a lion, Rumi says, but you won't bear the needle.
And a deaf man goes to visit a sick neighbor, rehearsing polite answers in advance, and gets every one hilariously, painfully wrong. Three stories; there are hundreds more.
Rumi breaks off some mid-way, doubles back, picks them up again later.
It's a book to live in, not to finish.
E. H. Whinfield's abridged English Masnavi from 1898 is old enough to be free to read, and Reynold Nicholson's full translation followed in the twentieth century.

how: Readers who love Rumi keep going through the Masnavi one story at a time, in Persian or in translation, often with a teacher or a reading circle, for years.

games.q: you're the man from Qazvin, under the tattoo artist's needle. it stings. what do you do?
o: bear it, and get the lion.
leave off the tail, then the ear, then the belly.
games.why: he asks to leave off part after part, until the artist throws down the needle: who ever saw a lion with no tail, no head and no belly?

practice: Let today's three stand in front of you: the grammarian in the storm, the man who wanted a lion but not the needle, the deaf visitor. Which one pricks you a little?
That's usually the next one to read; hold it, ask what it might say about you this week, and don't try to solve it.
